modelAnswer:
Two matrices are equal only if they have the same order AND every corresponding entry matches.

(a) $[x\ \ 9]=[2\ \ y]$: $x=2,\ y=9$

(b) $\begin{bmatrix}6&3\\4&x\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}7&3\\4&0\end{bmatrix}$: **not possible** -- the (1,1) entries $6\neq7$ already conflict, regardless of $x$.

(c) $\begin{bmatrix}5x\\2y\end{bmatrix}$ (order $2\times1$) $=[-10\ \ 20]$ (order $1\times2$): **not possible** -- the orders differ.

(d) $-\begin{bmatrix}2x&3y\\4z&10\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}8&6\\32&-10\end{bmatrix} \Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix}-2x&-3y\\-4z&-10\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}8&6\\32&-10\end{bmatrix}$: the $(2,2)$ entries match ($-10=-10$); $-2x=8\Rightarrow x=-4$; $-3y=6\Rightarrow y=-2$; $-4z=32\Rightarrow z=-8$.

(e) $\begin{bmatrix}x&-2y\\6&x+y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3&-6\\6&z\end{bmatrix}$: $x=3$; $-2y=-6\Rightarrow y=3$; $x+y=z\Rightarrow z=6$.

(f) $\begin{bmatrix}5\\6\\7\end{bmatrix}$ (order $3\times1$) $=\begin{bmatrix}5&0\\x&0\\7&0\end{bmatrix}$ (order $3\times2$): **not possible** -- the orders differ regardless of $x$.

(g) $\begin{bmatrix}x+y\\x-y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}11\\1\end{bmatrix}$: $x+y=11,\ x-y=1 \Rightarrow x=6,\ y=5$.

(h) $\begin{bmatrix}5&10\\15&x\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}5&y\\15&5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}z&15\\30&7\end{bmatrix} \Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix}10&10+y\\30&x+5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}z&15\\30&7\end{bmatrix}$: $z=10$; $10+y=15\Rightarrow y=5$; $x+5=7\Rightarrow x=2$.

(i) $4x+3y=-6,\ x+2y=1$. $A=\begin{bmatrix}4&3\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$, $|A|=8-3=5$. $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\\-1&4\end{bmatrix}$. $\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\\-1&4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-6\\1\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-15\\10\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3\\2\end{bmatrix}$. So $x=-3,\ y=2$.

(ii) $-x+2y=1.5,\ 5x+4y=3$. $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1&2\\5&4\end{bmatrix}$, $|A|=-4-10=-14$. $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{-14}\begin{bmatrix}4&-2\\-5&-1\end{bmatrix}$. $\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{-14}\begin{bmatrix}4&-2\\-5&-1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1.5\\3\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{-14}\begin{bmatrix}0\\-10.5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0.75\end{bmatrix}$. So $x=0,\ y=0.75$.

(iii) $2y=10-16x,\ 24x=15-3y$. Rearranged: $16x+2y=10$ (divide by 2: $8x+y=5$) and $24x+3y=15$ (divide by 3: $8x+y=5$). Both reduce to the **same equation**, so the coefficient matrix $\begin{bmatrix}16&2\\24&3\end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $48-48=0$: singular. Matrix inversion is **not possible**; the system has infinitely many solutions along $8x+y=5$.

(iv) $9-x=7y,\ 14y+2x=18$. Rearranged: $x+7y=9$ and $2x+14y=18$ (divide by 2: $x+7y=9$). Again the **same equation** twice, so $\begin{bmatrix}-1&-7\\2&14\end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $-14-(-14)=0$: singular. Matrix inversion is **not possible**; infinitely many solutions along $x+7y=9$.

**(b) Cramer's Rule**

(i) $2x+3y=5,\ 5x+10y=10$. $D=\begin{vmatrix}2&3\\5&10\end{vmatrix}=20-15=5$. $D_x=\begin{vmatrix}5&3\\10&10\end{vmatrix}=50-30=20$. $D_y=\begin{vmatrix}2&5\\5&10\end{vmatrix}=20-25=-5$. $x=20/5=4,\ y=-5/5=-1$.

keyPoints: A singular coefficient matrix (determinant zero) with proportional equations means the system is dependent, not solvable uniquely.
Check whether one equation is a scalar multiple of the other before assuming a unique matrix solution exists.
modelAnswer:
Let $l$ = labour cost rate per worker, $m$ = material cost rate per item (same rates for both industries).

Haani's: 6 workers, 80 items, total Rs. 20,000: $6l+80m=20000$.

Massab's: 12 workers, 160 items, total Rs. 40,000: $12l+160m=40000$.

Notice the second equation is exactly **twice** the first ($12=2\times6$, $160=2\times80$, $40000=2\times20000$). The coefficient matrix $\begin{bmatrix}6&80\\12&160\end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $6(160)-80(12)=960-960=0$, so it is singular.

The two equations are dependent (the same relationship scaled up), so the labour rate $l$ and material rate $m$ **cannot be uniquely determined** from this data alone; only their combination $6l+80m=20000$ is fixed, with infinitely many $(l,m)$ pairs satisfying it.

keyPoints: Matrix Inversion Method and Cramer's rule both require a non-singular coefficient matrix (determinant ≠ 0).
When both given equations reduce to the same line, the determinant is 0 and the system has infinitely many solutions rather than a unique pair.
modelAnswer:
**(a) Matrix Inversion Method**

(i) $4x+3y=-6,\ x+2y=1$. $A=\begin{bmatrix}4&3\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$, $|A|=8-3=5$. $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\\-1&4\end{bmatrix}$. $\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}2&-3\\-1&4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-6\\1\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-15\\10\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3\\2\end{bmatrix}$. So $x=-3,\ y=2$.

(ii) $-x+2y=1.5,\ 5x+4y=3$. $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1&2\\5&4\end{bmatrix}$, $|A|=-4-10=-14$. $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{-14}\begin{bmatrix}4&-2\\-5&-1\end{bmatrix}$. $\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{-14}\begin{bmatrix}4&-2\\-5&-1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1.5\\3\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{-14}\begin{bmatrix}0\\-10.5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0.75\end{bmatrix}$. So $x=0,\ y=0.75$.

(iii) $2y=10-16x,\ 24x=15-3y$. Rearranged: $16x+2y=10$ (divide by 2: $8x+y=5$) and $24x+3y=15$ (divide by 3: $8x+y=5$). Both reduce to the **same equation**, so the coefficient matrix $\begin{bmatrix}16&2\\24&3\end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $48-48=0$: singular. Matrix inversion is **not possible**; the system has infinitely many solutions along $8x+y=5$.

(iv) $9-x=7y,\ 14y+2x=18$. Rearranged: $x+7y=9$ and $2x+14y=18$ (divide by 2: $x+7y=9$). Again the **same equation** twice, so $\begin{bmatrix}-1&-7\\2&14\end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $-14-(-14)=0$: singular. Matrix inversion is **not possible**; infinitely many solutions along $x+7y=9$.

**(b) Cramer's Rule**

(i) $2x+3y=5,\ 5x+10y=10$. $D=\begin{vmatrix}2&3\\5&10\end{vmatrix}=20-15=5$. $D_x=\begin{vmatrix}5&3\\10&10\end{vmatrix}=50-30=20$. $D_y=\begin{vmatrix}2&5\\5&10\end{vmatrix}=20-25=-5$. $x=20/5=4,\ y=-5/5=-1$.

(ii) $x=\frac{2}{3}-2y \Rightarrow x+2y=\frac{2}{3}$; $4y=3-3x \Rightarrow 3x+4y=3$. $D=\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{vmatrix}=4-6=-2$. $D_x=\begin{vmatrix}2/3&2\\3&4\end{vmatrix}=8/3-6=-10/3$. $D_y=\begin{vmatrix}1&2/3\\3&3\end{vmatrix}=3-2=1$. $x=\frac{-10/3}{-2}=\frac{5}{3},\ y=\frac{1}{-2}=-\frac{1}{2}$.

(iii) $\frac{6}{10}x+\frac{8}{10}y=20 \Rightarrow 0.6x+0.8y=20$; $\frac{8}{10}x-\frac{6}{10}y=10 \Rightarrow 0.8x-0.6y=10$. $D=\begin{vmatrix}0.6&0.8\\0.8&-0.6\end{vmatrix}=-0.36-0.64=-1$. $D_x=\begin{vmatrix}20&0.8\\10&-0.6\end{vmatrix}=-12-8=-20$. $D_y=\begin{vmatrix}0.6&20\\0.8&10\end{vmatrix}=6-16=-10$. $x=-20/-1=20,\ y=-10/-1=10$.

(iv) $16x-10+2y=0 \Rightarrow 16x+2y=10$; $15-3y-24x=0 \Rightarrow 24x+3y=15$. Dividing gives $8x+y=5$ in both cases: the **same equation**, so $D=\begin{vmatrix}16&2\\24&3\end{vmatrix}=48-48=0$. Cramer's rule **fails** (D = 0); infinitely many solutions along $8x+y=5$.
